young.html: William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, England, in 1564. He went to London, became an actor, and wrote about 38 plays and many poems. Four hundred years later, people all over the world still act them.

His comedies are not just jokes. They are stories where everything gets mixed up and then comes right at the end, usually with a wedding (or three). In A Midsummer Night's Dream, four young people run away into an enchanted wood. A mischievous fairy named Puck uses a magic flower to make people fall in love with the wrong person, and gives a weaver named Bottom a donkey's head!

young.html: Shakespeare's plays were acted in an open-air theater called the Globe. Some people sat in covered galleries. Others paid a penny to stand in the yard right next to the stage.

young.html: Put on a scene. The workmen in A Midsummer Night's Dream put on a play so badly that it becomes a comedy: one of them plays a wall, and another plays the moonshine. Choose a simple story (the three little pigs, perhaps) and act it with your family, with people playing the scenery too. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

full.html: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was a glover's son from Stratford-upon-Avon. By the early 1590s he was in London as an actor and playwright, and from 1594 he was a member and part-owner of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later the King's Men. In 1599 the company built the Globe on the south bank of the Thames. Plays were acted in daylight, with little scenery and with boys in the women's parts. In 1623, seven years after his death, two fellow actors gathered 36 of his plays in the First Folio.

full.html: Three worlds meet in the wood: the young Athenian lovers, the fairy court of Oberon and Titania, and the "rude mechanicals," workmen rehearsing a play for the Duke's wedding. Puck's mistakes with the love-flower make the lovers swap and quarrel. The fairy queen, under the same spell, falls in love with Bottom. By morning, all is set right.

full.text:
Shall we their fond pageant see?
Lord, what fools these mortals be!
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.work: A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act III, scene 2 (Puck)
full.ed: First printed in the First Folio
full.note: "Fond" here means foolish. Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: Notice the rhythm: the fairies often speak in short, chanting, rhymed lines, while the lovers speak in longer verse and the workmen in prose. Shakespeare gives each world its own music.

full.text:
All the world's a stage,
And all the men and women merely players;
They have their exits and their entrances,
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.work: As You Like It, Act II, scene 7 (Jaques)
full.ed: First printed in the First Folio
full.note: Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: Jaques goes on to describe the "seven ages" of a life, from infant to old age. It is a melancholy speech in a happy play, and a good example of how the comedies make room for sadness too.

Thinking a comedy must be all jokes. In Shakespeare, "comedy" means a story that moves from trouble to harmony. Several comedies have dark moments, and The Merchant of Venice has troubled many modern readers for how it treats Shylock, its Jewish moneylender.

deep.html: Rosalind, Viola and Portia are among the cleverest people in their plays, and all three spend much of the play dressed as young men. On Shakespeare's stage, where boys played women, this meant a boy playing a woman playing a man. Readers still discuss what the disguises let these heroines say and do.

deep.html: Earlier on this ladder, Aristophanes wrote the comedies of ancient Athens; Erasmus's Folly speaks like Shakespeare's wise fools. Later, Molière's comedies in France take up the same tangles of love and pretense.

questions: Puck says "Lord, what fools these mortals be!" When have you seen people act foolishly because of love or friendship?
Why do you think so many of Shakespeare's heroines wear disguises?
If you could stand in the Globe's yard for a penny, would you? What would be fun about it, and what would not?
Jaques says all the world's a stage. What part are you playing right now?
